clinicalPearls: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2, also called Gordon syndrome or familial hyperkalaemic hypertension, is caused by variants in WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 or CUL3 that increase activity of the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
The characteristic combination is hypertension with hyperkalaemia and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, essentially the mirror image of Gitelman syndrome
Renin is suppressed while aldosterone is variable, and importantly hyperkalaemia occurs despite a normal glomerular filtration rate
Excess distal sodium-chloride reabsorption expands volume and reduces the sodium delivery needed for distal potassium and hydrogen secretion, causing potassium and acid retention
It responds strikingly to a thiazide diuretic, which inhibits the overactive cotransporter and corrects both the blood pressure and the electrolyte abnormalities
The KLHL3 and CUL3 variants disrupt the ubiquitin-mediated degradation of WNK kinases, increasing their signalling to the cotransporter
Consider it in patients with hyperkalaemia and hypertension that seem out of proportion to renal function
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 results from dysregulation of the WNK kinase signalling network that controls the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Variants in WNK1 or WNK4, or in the KLHL3 and CUL3 components of the ubiquitin ligase complex that normally degrades WNK kinases, lead to excessive kinase activity and increased cotransporter abundance and function. Enhanced distal sodium-chloride reabsorption expands extracellular volume and raises blood pressure, and by consuming luminal sodium it reduces the electrochemical driving force for potassium and hydrogen secretion in the downstream nephron. The net effect is salt-dependent, low-renin hypertension with hyperkalaemia and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, which is reversed by inhibiting the cotransporter with a thiazide.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic kidney disease with hyperkalaemia and hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium, chloride and bicarbonate to define hyperkalaemic hyperchloraemic acidosis
Renal function to demonstrate hyperkalaemia despite preserved glomerular filtration
Review of medications that raise potassium
Assessment of blood-pressure and biochemical response to thiazide therapy
Molecular genetic testing of WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 and CUL3
redFlags: Family history of early hypertension with hyperkalaemia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally excellent because low-dose thiazide therapy typically normalises blood pressure and electrolytes; untreated disease carries the usual cardiovascular risks of hypertension and the hazards of hyperkalaemia.
pitfalls: Attributing hyperkalaemia to renal failure when the glomerular filtration rate is actually preserved
Prescribing renin-angiotensin blockade for the hypertension, which can worsen the hyperkalaemia
Missing the diagnosis by not recognising the mirror-image relationship to Gitelman syndrome
Overlooking the excellent and specific response to thiazide treatment
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
management: Thiazide diuretic as specific therapy, correcting both the hypertension and the hyperkalaemic hyperchloraemic acidosis by inhibiting the overactive sodium-chloride cotransporter
Dietary sodium and chloride restriction to complement the thiazide effect
Reduce dietary potassium and withdraw drugs that raise serum potassium
Monitor blood pressure, electrolytes and acid-base status in response to treatment
Manage the broader cardiovascular risk associated with hypertension
Genetic counselling and family screening for variants in WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 and CUL3
